name: Awbrey Butte
label: Awbrey Butte
about_prose: Ask what Awbrey Butte actually offers and the answer is elevation. The butte is the highest landmass inside Bend's city limits, its summit at 4,230 feet, sitting in the city's northwest quadrant about 3 miles from downtown by way of NW Newport Avenue. Homes on the west side look across the Cascade Range from Mount Jefferson to Mount Bachelor. Homes on the east side look down on downtown's grid, the Old Mill smokestacks, and Pilot Butte. The drive to downtown runs about 10 minutes, Old Mill District about 12, and Mount Bachelor about 25 by way of Cascade Lakes Highway. That combination, close enough for a weeknight dinner downtown, high enough to sit above the traffic and the noise, is what people are actually buying when they buy on the butte.

The neighborhood exists because Brooks Resources bought 1,800 acres on the butte in 1970 and treated it as a decades-long project rather than a quick build-out. The company broke ground on homesites in 1984 and kept building until the last of 782 homesites was in place by 2005. The design choices from that process still define the place: large lots that leave mature ponderosa pines standing, roads routed around the hillside so they stay largely out of view from below, and a house-color requirement that limits new construction to earth-tone exteriors. It is a low-density neighborhood built inside a city, on purpose, not a subdivision that happened to end up wooded.

Buying here means buying into a planned community under the Oregon Planned Community Act, with CC&Rs and bylaws recorded against the deed. New construction and most exterior changes go through the Awbrey Butte Owners Association's Architectural Review Committee before anyone breaks ground, and a board of elected homeowner volunteers, working with a managing agent, handles common-area maintenance and collects assessments. Want to paint your house a color outside the approved earth-tone range, or add on in a style the committee does not like, that review is the trade-off for the wooded, low-density feel the whole neighborhood is built around. The association also carries a Firewise USA designation, awarded in 2019, with a volunteer committee trained by the Department of Forestry, the Fire Marshal, and Tamarack Wildfire offering free defensible-space assessments to homeowners, worth noting on a forested hillside in a fire-prone part of the state.

Two Bend Park and Recreation District parks sit on top of the butte itself: Sylvan Park, 3.8 acres at 2996 NW 3 Sisters Drive, and Summit Park, 3.8 acres at 1150 NW Promontory Drive, each with tennis courts and connected by an unpaved trail. For a longer walk, the Deschutes River Trail's Awbrey Reach runs 3.9 miles of compacted gravel along the canyon rim on the butte's northeastern edge, built on top of the buried Tumalo Canal irrigation right-of-way, with views out to Black Butte, Mount Jefferson, and the Sisters. Access is the catch. The main trailhead is Sawyer Park to the south, and parking near the neighborhood end of the trail, closer to Awbrey Glen, is limited, so most people drive to the trailhead rather than walk out their door to reach it. Awbrey Glen Golf Club, an 18-hole private course designed by Gene Mason in 1993 and later updated by David McLay Kidd, plays 7,007 yards along the butte's southwestern edge. It is membership-only, not a perk that comes free with the address.
The K-5 school built into the neighborhood is High Lakes Elementary at 2500 NW High Lakes Loop, part of Bend-La Pine Schools, feeding into Cascade Middle School and then Summit High School.

Put together, Awbrey Butte suits someone who wants mature trees, a low-density street, and a long Cascades view inside city limits, and who does not mind a design committee having a say in how the house looks from the road. It suits a buyer less well if what they actually want is a trail out the back gate or full control over their own exterior. Both of those trade-offs are the direct result of the same decisions, made in 1970 and enforced ever since, that make the neighborhood what it is.

amenities.name: Sylvan Park
amenities.description: A 3.8-acre park at 2996 NW 3 Sisters Drive atop the butte, with two tennis courts, a playground, and over half the site left in natural woods. Acquired from Brooks Resources in 1988.

amenities.name: Summit Park
amenities.description: A 3.8-acre park at 1150 NW Promontory Drive with two tennis courts, a half-court, open lawn, and an unpaved trail connecting to Sylvan Park.

amenities.name: Awbrey Glen Golf Club
amenities.description: An 18-hole private club at 2500 NW Awbrey Glen Drive, designed by Gene Mason in 1993 and updated by David McLay Kidd, playing 7,007 yards through pines and rock outcrops.

amenities.name: High Lakes Elementary
amenities.description: The Bend-La Pine Schools K-5 serving Awbrey Butte, at 2500 NW High Lakes Loop. Students continue to Cascade Middle and Summit High.

amenities.name: Awbrey Butte Summit
amenities.description: The butte's summit at 4,230 feet is the highest point within Bend's city limits, giving the neighborhood its elevation and views.

drive_times.note: 3 miles south via NW Newport Avenue
